description: We are CC, a two person team trying to expand our skills and knowledge by creating a meaningful storytelling solution that will impact and encourage youth to have a curious mind that is excited about discovery.
summary: Our project — The Forgotten Heroes: A Discovery — is a browser-based game that takes users into space and allows them to explore the forgotten equipment left up there. It shows them the history and objectives of these missions, how they ended up there, and why they were forgotten and abandoned, involving multi-choice quizzes and gamification to provide a fun learning environment. It serves as an avenue for students new to the topic to get interested, or as an entertaining resource for intrigued students and teachers alike, without the verbosity of articles.
details:
1. Problem statement

Every Moon and Mars mission relied on equipment that was left behind once its job was done, and most of it is now forgotten. We identified three problems:

  1. Few people know the equipment behind the missions. Everyone has heard of the Moon landing, but not of the rovers, landers and science packages that made it and the Mars missions possible.
  2. Learning about it is tough. The information is spread across long, technical articles that are tedious and wordy, especially for young readers.
  3. Students need a fun way to learn; They need something that holds their attention and leaves them curious to find out more.

The Forgotten Heroes: A Discovery answers each of these problems.

2. Overview

The Forgotten Heroes: A Discovery is a browser game that introduces the equipment behind NASA's Moon and Mars missions to people who have never heard of it. Players learn through a story alongside Nova, a curious and somewhat-nerdy NASA intern who is just as eager to find out as they are. Each abandoned machine becomes a character with its own personality, so its story is memorable.

Nova gives the player a task: to accompany her to explore space and collect 60 research points by finding out about the equipment left behind. Every piece of equipment has its own voice and attitude, and it banters with Nova as the player reads its story in short, bite-sized lines.

How a player moves through the game:

  1. Meet Nova: she introduces herself, explains why the forgotten equipment matters, points to the research points counter and asks if the player is ready.
  2. Choose a planet: the Moon or Mars. Each holds three pieces of equipment.
  3. Meet the equipment: short descriptions alternate with back-and-forth conversations between Nova and the machine. An "i" card shows real photos and extra facts.
  4. Take the quiz: a multiple-choice question (A–D) for each piece of equipment. A correct answer earns 10 research points. A wrong answer means redoing the quiz, with no penalty.
  5. Bonus: when all 60 points are collected, Nova announces she sees something (a bonus). Pioneer 10 appears in open space.
  6. Thank you: after the bonus, Nova thanks the player and shares what she has learnt, followed by the team credits.

Equipment featured:

  1. Moon: Apollo Lunar Modules · Lunar Roving Vehicles (LRVs) · ALSEP Scientific Packages
  2. Mars: Spirit & Opportunity · Viking 1 Lander · InSight Lander
  3. Open space: Pioneer 10

3. Aim and objectives

Aim: make the forgotten equipment behind NASA's Moon and Mars missions known and easy to learn about for all ages, with pre-teens as the main audience and teachers as a ready-made classroom resource, making an originally tiring task much more fun.

Objectives:

  1. Raise awareness of the equipment (problem 1): feature seven pieces of real, discarded NASA hardware across the Moon, Mars and open space, each with its own story, photos and facts.
  2. Replace long articles with short dialogue (problem 2): deliver the facts as bite-sized descriptions and back-and-forth conversations between Nova and the equipment, written for younger readers.
  3. Make learning fun and rewarding (problem 3): use gamification, with research points, a progress counter, a quiz per piece of equipment, no-penalty retries and an unlockable bonus.
  4. Build curiosity, not just memory (problem 3): through Nova, a curious intern who asks the questions players are likely to have, model the habit of asking "why?" and "what happened next?".
  5. Make it easy to access and adapt: a free browser game with no sign-up or install, whose text and quizzes teachers can edit without touching code.

4. Tech stack

The game is a static website: it runs entirely in the browser, with no server, database or log-in.

  • IDE: Kiro
  • Languages: TypeScript (React TSX), CSS, HTML, JSON 
  • Framework and build: React 19, Vite (build tool and dev server), Node.js 20+
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS v4
  • Animation: Motion (motion/react) for all transitions; Aceternity UI typewriter effect for the title
  • Soundtrack, sound effects and audio: elevenlabs.io & pixabay
  • Dev tools: sharp (generates the custom cursor sizes), TypeScript compiler, oxlint
  • Fonts: Title: NEOTERIC, Text: Electrolize
  • Assets: original illustrations by the team (Nova, planets, rocket, equipment, cursor, research points icon), exported at three resolutions (x1, x2, x3)
  • Hosting: Github pages

5. Tools used

  • Figma
  • Procreate
  • Claude
  • Claude code
  • Kiro

6. Key technical innovations

Each technical choice serves the problem: 

  • Content without code. All dialogs, descriptions, quizzes and credits live in plain JSON files. Teachers or students can add a line, a question or a whole new piece of equipment by editing a text file. The points goal recalculates itself, and mistakes show up as a clear on-screen message instead of a broken page.
  • A living character from layered sprites. Nova is built from separate body, eyes, brows and mouth layers. Each line of dialog picks an expression (happy, sad, confused, excited and more). She blinks on her own, and her mouth moves only while her words are typing out.
  • Characters with voices. As each line types, short voice blips play with a slightly random pitch, giving Nova and every piece of equipment their own voice without recorded speech. Buttons, transitions, correct and wrong answers and earned points all have sound effects.
  • Sharp on any screen. Every image comes in three resolutions. The game measures how large each image is actually drawn, including mid-zoom, and loads the sharper version in the background before swapping, so nothing flashes.
  • A drifting starfield. An oversized star layer scrolls endlessly, giving the feeling of travelling through space.
  • Drop-in assets. Artists save images and sounds into named folders, and the game finds them automatically whatever the file type.
  • Runs anywhere, costs nothing. A static site on GitHub Pages: no server, no accounts, no installing needed. Layouts scale to any screen with the 16:9 frame kept, and it supports keyboard controls and reduced-motion settings.

7. Benefits

The game answers each problem directly:

  1. Few people know the equipment behind the missions

How The Forgotten Heroes: A Discovery solves it

Puts seven forgotten machines as the focus. Each one is a character with a personality and real NASA photos, so players remember it the way they remember a person.

  1. Learning from articles is tedious and wordy

How The Forgotten Heroes: A Discovery solves it

Breaks the facts into short lines that type out one at a time, mixed with conversation and humour. Players read at their own pace, and an "i" card holds the extra detail for those who want more.

  1. Students need a fun way to learn that builds curiosity

How The Forgotten Heroes: A Discovery solves it

Turns learning into a mission: 60 research points to collect, quizzes with instant feedback and free retries, and a hidden bonus to unlock. Nova asks the questions a curious student would, showing that not knowing is the start of discovering.

8. Target Audience

For students (pre-teens and up): they learn real space history through story and play rather than textbooks, stay motivated by a clear goal and rewards, and come away curious about the missions and machines they met.

For teachers: a free resource that works in any modern browser, including school laptops and Chromebooks, with no accounts or installs. It can be used in class or as homework, and the text and quizzes can be edited to fit a lesson or age group.

For the challenge theme: it gives a voice to equipment usually left out of mission stories, showing that "abandoned" hardware still matters. Some of it, like the Apollo-era science packages, kept sending data long after the astronauts went home.


9. Future Enhancements

  • An automatic save system that allows for users to save their progress when reloading or exiting the site.
  • A content expansion consisting of more examples of abandoned technology on each planet and beyond.
  • More gamemode updates beyond just quizzes and back-and-forth dialogue
  • A log in/sign in page for users to track their progress.
  • A local leaderboard for accuracy, amount of times completed, etc.
